newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-WILLIAMS HOMER LIFTS YANKS PAST ORIOLES IN 11TH. [CORRECTED 03:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-WILLIAMS HOMER LIFTS YANKS PAST ORIOLES IN 11TH. [CORRECTED 03:05 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects throughout that Tony Tarasco rather than Mike Devereaux was right fielder)
By Gary Hill

Derek Jeter hit a controversial game-tying home run in the eighth inning, and Bernie Williams's towering homer in the 11th gave the New York Yankees a 5-4 victory over the Baltimore Orioles in the opening game of their American League Championship Series on Wednesday.
Jeter's homer was swatted by a young fan in the stands before Baltimore right fielder Tony Tarasco could catch it.
"I was camped under the ball," said Tarasco. "It was a routine fly ball."
He added: "To me it was a magic trick, because the ball just disappeared out of thin air."
But there was nothing controversial about the Williams blast, which came on a 1-1 pitch leading off the 11th inning.
"Anybody see a replay of Bernie's home run?" New York manager Joe Torre joked. "That wasn't bad."
The Yankees took advantage of Oriole fielding blunders to score their first two runs.
In the first inning, B.J. Surhoff lost Tim Raines's easy pop fly to left, giving him a double and allowing him to score on a Williams ground-out.
After Cal Ripken doubled and an Eddie Murray ground-out scored him in the second inning to tie the game at 1-1, the Yankees again capitalised on poor Baltimore glove work.

The normally slick-fielding second baseman Roberto Alomar -- booed at every at-bat for his spitting incident with umpire John Hirschbeck -- had a grounder from Paul O'Neill graze off his glove, then bounced the throw for an error.

That put men on first and second with none out. Alomar made a nifty backhand flip to start a probable double play on a Mariano Duncan grounder, but Ripken's throw to first drew Rafael Palmeiro off the bag, and Baltimore got only one out, leaving men on first and third.
Jim Leyritz's grounder scored Cecil Fielder, who had led off the inning with a walk.
Brady Anderson and Rafael Palmeiro homered to lead off the third and fourth innings to put Baltimore up 3-2.

Palmeiro scored three times and had three hits and two walks in a perfect night at the plate for Baltimore, which added another run in the sixth on Surhoff's sacrifice fly scoring Palmeiro after Yankee starter Andy Pettitte had loaded the bases on two walks and a Ripken single.
New York got another gift and cut the lead to 4-3 in the seventh when pinch-hitter Darryl Strawberry walked with the bases loaded, the third free pass of the inning.
The key play came when Bonilla leaped to catch Williams's fly ball at the right-field wall, but lost it as he came down into the wall, giving Williams a double.
Then came the game-tying homer by Jeter, who went 4-for-5 for the Yankees.

Twelve-year-old Jeff Maier reached out his glove and batted Jeter's fly ball back into the stands as Tarasco, just inserted for defensive purposes in the top of the inning, waited for it to come down.

Tarasco immediately complained it should have been fan interference but right-field umpire and crew chief Rich Garcia's home run call stood despite a lengthy argument between the Orioles and umpires in right field, as fans threw down objects and pieces of paper.
